title: Pauri 28, sound: mundaa santokh

lines: ASH, A COAT, RINGS IN THE EARS.
cards: Ash on the skin. Matted hair. A patched coat, a bag over the shoulder, and in each ear a heavy ring.
In Guru Nanak's time, that outfit marked the Nath yogis, wandering ascetics who left home to master body and mind. You could tell who they were before they said a word.
Tradition says Guru Nanak met and talked with yogis like these more than once on his travels. The next four stanzas of Japji speak to them, in their own language, using the very things they carried.

teach.b: The first line of Pauri 28, in the original: mundaa santokh saram pat jholee dhiaan kee karahi bibhoot. Word by word. Mundaa, MOON-daa: earrings, the large rings of the yogi.

Santokh, sun-TOKH: contentment, the word from day one hundred eighty, enough, by listening. Saram, SUH-rum: effort, or modesty; commentators read it both ways. Pat: honor, the word from Pauri 14, going forth with honor.
Jholee, JHO-lee: the pouch or begging bag the yogi carries. Dhiaan: meditation, attention. Bibhoot, bi-BHOOT: the ashes the yogis smeared on their bodies.
So the line is built from pieces of the yogi's outfit, earrings, bag, ashes, each paired with an inner quality. What that pairing means comes tomorrow. Today, notice the craft.
Guru Nanak doesn't argue with the yogis in abstract terms. He picks up the very objects they carry and speaks through them. One more sound to listen for.
Each of these four stanzas, 28 to 31, ends with the same words: aades tisai aades. Commentators explain that aades was the greeting the Nath yogis used with each other.
So Guru Nanak even closes in their greeting, and turns it: salutation to Him, salutation to the One.
Mundaa santokh. Earrings, contentment. The outfit, and what it could mean.

how: Pauri 28 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; pauris 28 to 31 are addressed to the yogis, and each ends with aades tisai aades, salutation to Him.

o: salutation, the Nath yogis' own greeting
a farewell yogis said on leaving camp
a blessing a guru gives a new student

games.q: the yogi's outfit in Pauri 28 — tap the pairs.

s: Pauri 28 argues with the yogis in abstract terms

games.q: you want to speak to wandering yogis about what matters. how does Guru Nanak begin Pauri 28?
o: by telling them to go home.
by naming their earrings, bag and ashes, each paired with an inner quality.
games.why: mundaa santokh saram pat jholee dhiaan kee karahi bibhoot: he speaks in their own things, and even closes in their own greeting.

practice: Say the first line aloud, slowly: mundaa santokh, saram pat jholee, dhiaan kee karahi bibhoot. Say it again a little quieter, then a third time with only the first two words, mundaa santokh.
Then sit, and let santokh, contentment, rest where earrings would rest, close to your ears, close to what you hear.

wordCard.voice: Aades, salutation, the yogis' own greeting. It opens mundaa santokh: earrings of contentment, a bag of effort and honor, ashes of meditation.
